summary: A collapsible Sidebar.Section now animates its height instead of snapping. It opened and closed with the `hidden` attribute, while Accordion — the identical interaction one component over — animated against the measurement Base UI publishes; two answers to one question is the divergence this library records rather than keeps. The section moves onto Base UI's Collapsible (ADR 0012) and transitions `height` to `--collapsible-panel-height` at motionStandard, exactly as Accordion's panel does: `height: auto` cannot be transitioned and a constant would clip a section with more rows than the artboard drew. The reason to take the behaviour layer's answer rather than write a third is not the height, which is easy — it is the ORDERING. `hidden` must stay off until the closing animation finishes, or the rows blank before the space closes, and must go back on afterwards, or a collapsed section is flat but still in the tab order. `keepMounted` is set because aria-controls must point at something that exists. One regression was introduced and caught while building it: rendering the panel with our own `id` overrode the id Base UI had generated and already pointed aria-controls at, leaving the trigger referencing an element that did not exist — a broken disclosure that looked completely normal, since the attribute was present and the panel still opened. A test asserting that aria-controls RESOLVES, rather than merely exists, is added alongside. A non-collapsible section is untouched and carries none of this machinery.

migration.manual: The expanded and collapsed end states are pixel-identical — the sidebar visual baseline did not move — so nothing static changes. What changes is between them, plus two things worth knowing if you test or style this. The panel's `id` is now generated by the behaviour layer rather than by us, so do not select on it (use `[data-slot="sidebar-sublist"]`); and `hidden` now arrives AFTER the collapse animation rather than with the click, so a test asserting it immediately must await the animation first.
